approval.cost: No fee for API keys, OAuth client registration, embed secrets, or Google OAuth configuration is stated in the documentation read (Looker instance licensing itself is outside the pages read)
approval.trigger: Vendor (Google/Looker) review: none documented. No app review, approval queue, marketplace listing, or partner certification is described for API keys, OAuth client app registrations, embed secrets, or Google Authentication; nothing is submitted to Google for approval. The customer's own admins approve throughout: API keys and embed secrets are created by the customer's Looker admin inside the customer's instance; OAuth client apps are registered per instance; Google OAuth is configured by the customer's Google Workspace/GCP admin using the customer's own Google Cloud project. Each customer is a separate manual setup. One stated cap: signed embed session length, 'Maximum session length accepted is 2592000 seconds (30 days)'. The only propagation figure stated: after adding a redirect URI to a Looker (Google Cloud core) OAuth client, 'It may take from five minutes to a few hours for the update to take effect'.

blockers.detail: Every credential is minted inside each customer's instance by that customer's admin and handed over out-of-band. A 'Connect your Looker' button cannot be fully self-serve for the end user in the documented model.
blockers.howToClear: Build an admin-guided onboarding flow and a secure credential intake (client ID, client secret, and the per-customer API Host URL).
blockers.title: No cross-customer consent flow

blockers.detail: Keys act with the permissions of the user they're attached to; a service-account key means 'all users share the same level of access'. Row/column-level LookML security is only respected when acting with a target user's own access token (login_user / OAuth client), which is the multi-tenant-safe pattern.
blockers.howToClear: Use a least-privilege dedicated service user, and prefer per-user token patterns where row-level security matters.
blockers.title: API-key power equals the key owner's power

blockers.detail: The embed secret is a single, instance-wide secret; 'To change your secret, select the Reset Secret button, you should be aware that this will break any existing signed embeds', and 'Resetting the JWT token will invalidate all active cookieless embed sessions'. Algorithm trap: secrets created via the Admin Embed page use HMAC-SHA1, while secrets created via the create_embed_secret API endpoint default to HMAC-SHA256; the signing script must match.
blockers.howToClear: Coordinate any secret reset with the customer's admin and expect embed downtime; record which creation path (and algorithm) each customer's secret used.
blockers.title: Embed secret rotation is destructive

flavor.recommended: A per-customer API key on a dedicated API-only service-account user in the customer's Looker instance
flavor.why: Looker has no global third-party OAuth app program: no Looker-operated developer portal where a SaaS registers once and arbitrary customers authorize it via a Looker-hosted consent screen. The documented connection objects are all per-instance: an API key (a client_id + client_secret pair generated on a user in the customer's instance; 'The client credentials required for this login must be obtained by creating an API key on a user account in the Looker Admin console'), a per-instance OAuth client app registration, an embed secret, and a Google OAuth client (for instance sign-in). Google's Conversational Analytics authentication doc has a row for exactly the recommended pattern: 'Looker API-only service account | API key | Client ID and secret', noting 'All users share the same level of access to Looker'. The customer admin creates the service user and key; the SaaS exchanges them at the instance's /login endpoint for an access token.

humanMust: (Customer's Looker admin) Create a dedicated API/service user in the customer's instance with a role carrying the needed permissions
(Customer's Looker admin) Generate an API key on that user (Admin > Users > Edit User > API Keys > Edit Keys > New API key)
(Customer's Looker admin) Hand the client ID + client secret and the instance API Host URL to the SaaS out-of-band
name: Looker
nuances: Header quirk: 'The access token returned by login must be used in the HTTP Authorization header of subsequent API requests, like this: Authorization: token <access_token>' (the literal word 'token', not Bearer). Best practice for /login: 'Always pass credentials in body params.'

Instance URL/port variance: Google Cloud/Azure and newer AWS instances use port 443; older AWS-hosted instances may use port 19999. Collect the correct API Host URL per customer (Admin > API); format is https://<instance_name>.cloud.looker.com on Google Cloud.

Signed embedding figures (provider-stated): session_length 'Defaults to 300 seconds. Maximum session length accepted is 2592000 seconds (30 days)'; 'An embed URL can only be used once, and must be used within 5 minutes of being created'; the nonce 'cannot be repeated within an hour'. Embed users are not OAuth users: permissions/models/groups are asserted by the SaaS in the signed URL, reusing one external_user_id across different people or permission sets 'can cause data to be visible to users who otherwise wouldn't have access to it', and 'No changes can be made to a user's permissions or user attributes mid-session'.

OAuth client app registration is a kill switch: 'When enabled is true, OAuth2 and API requests will be accepted from this app. When false, all requests from this app will be refused. Setting disabled invalidates existing tokens.' The tokens_invalid_before field invalidates 'All auth codes, access tokens, and refresh tokens issued for this application prior to this date-time for ALL USERS'. Registration mismatch is treated as forgery: 'If the client_guid and redirect_uri parameters in the login request do not match the app details registered with the Looker instance, the request is assumed to be a forgery and is rejected'.

Google OAuth (instance sign-in) is one-way and domain-wide: 'All users in the specified domain get access to the Looker instance'; 'New Looker accounts that authenticate using Google OAuth cannot switch to password authentication, even if OAuth is disabled for the Looker instance'; a deleted Google Cloud project hosting the OAuth client can cause a '401 deleted_client' lockout (Google recommends enabling 'Alternate login for admins' as a fallback).
prerequisites: A customer Looker admin willing to create the service user and API key
The per-customer API Host URL (Admin > API)
A secure way to receive and store the client ID + client secret

steps.detail: Admin > Users: create a dedicated API/service user and give it a role with the needed permissions. Google's audit-log integration doc models this same service-account-user pattern.
steps.title: (Customer admin) Create a dedicated API/service user

steps.detail: 'To generate API keys, in the API Keys section of the Admin > Users > Edit User page, click the Edit Keys button... Click the New API key button to generate a new key.' (On Looker (Google Cloud core), admins instead enable individual users to manage their own API keys from their Account page.) Hand the client ID + client secret and the API Host URL (Admin > API) to the SaaS.
steps.title: (Customer admin) Generate an API key; hand off credentials

steps.detail: POST /api/4.0/login with the client_id and client_secret in body params ('Looker API implements the OAuth2 Resource Owner Password Credentials Grant pattern'). The response returns access_token, token_type, expires_in, and a refresh_token for obtaining a new access token.
steps.title: Exchange the key at /login for an access token

steps.detail: Send 'Authorization: token <access_token>' on every request (literal 'token', not Bearer). Refresh via the refresh_token before expiry.
steps.title: Call the API (Authorization: token header)

steps.detail: Register the app with the customer's instance via the Register OAuth App API endpoint or the API Explorer extension, supplying a unique client_guid and redirect_uri (a group_id can restrict which Looker users may use the app). Users then sign in with OAuth against the instance to get access tokens that respect their own LookML permissions.
steps.title: Alternative: register an OAuth client app with the instance

tagline: Looker runs no global OAuth app program either: the working credential is a per-instance API key on a customer-created service user, exchanged at the instance's /login endpoint. Everything is created by the customer's own admins, with no vendor review, and the multi-tenant-safe patterns are per-user tokens, not the shared key.

time.active: ~15 min of customer-admin setup per instance + ~1 hr of login code
time.total: Same day per customer (no vendor wait at all)
